did_you_know.text: Did you know? After Abner’s death, Ish-bosheth became weak, and all Israel was alarmed. This highlights Abner’s central role in supporting Ish-bosheth’s kingdom.
Did you know? Rechab and Baanah were sons of Rimmon the Beerothite and served as commanders of divisions in Ish-bosheth’s army. The text notes that Beeroth was considered part of Benjamin.
Did you know? The people of Beeroth fled to Gittaim and lived there as resident foreigners until the time when this account was written, as the text states.
Did you know? Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s son and Saul’s grandson, was injured in his feet as a child when his nurse carried him while fleeing after news of Saul and Jonathan’s deaths became known.
Did you know? Rechab and Baanah came to Ish-bosheth’s house in the heat of the day, while he was lying down for his midday rest.
Did you know? The text describes Rechab and Baanah as entering Ish-bosheth’s house under the pretense of getting wheat; afterward, they struck him in his bedroom.
Did you know? After killing Ish-bosheth and cutting off his head, Rechab and Baanah fled all night along the road through the Arabah to Hebron.
Did you know? The killers tried to present Ish-bosheth’s death to David as revenge against his enemy and as an act carried out by the Lord, but David rejected their claim.

Did you know? David recalled the Amalekite young man who brought him news of Saul’s death and whom he killed at Ziklag; in this way, he made clear that killing a rival is not an act deserving a reward.
Did you know? David ordered Rechab and Baanah to be executed, while he ordered Ish-bosheth’s head to be buried in Abner’s tomb in Hebron.
